questions.scenario: You are setting up a new account for a simple mobile application.
questions.hint: Look for the most common sequence of numbers used globally.

candidates.explanation: This is one of the most common passwords in the world and is the first thing attackers try.
A combination of words and numbers that is significantly harder to guess than a sequence.
A random string of mixed characters provides high entropy.
A long passphrase is generally strong against brute-force attacks.

questions.scenario: You are creating a password for your corporate work email account.
questions.hint: Substituting letters for symbols (like '@' for 'a') is a technique attackers have already automated.

candidates.explanation: Common substitutions (Leet speak) are easily cracked by modern dictionary attacks.
While it uses substitutions, its length and added date make it stronger than a basic 'password' variation.
Passphrases with delimiters are resistant to simple dictionary attacks.
Randomized character sets provide high resistance to guessing.

questions.scenario: You are choosing a master password for a high-security encrypted vault.
questions.hint: Complexity does not always equal security; some 'complex' passwords are famous in leak databases.

candidates.explanation: Despite the symbols and numbers, this is a very common password found in massive breach lists (RockYou), making it a target for attackers.
High randomness and length make this extremely difficult to crack via brute force.
High length (entropy) makes this password very strong against most attack vectors.
An unpredictable mix of characters provides strong security.
